name: Microsoft Certified: Information Security Administrator Associate
title: Practice Exam 1
note: Microsoft scores SC-401 on a 1–1000 scale with 700 to pass. This practice exam reports a straight percentage; treat 80% as your readiness bar.

cs.title: Case Study — Northwind Traders (Legal Services)
cs.body:
Northwind Traders is a legal services firm with 1,500 employees on Microsoft 365 E5.

• Client matter numbers stored in a SQL database (format: MATTER-XXXXXX)
• NDA templates and legal briefs stored in SharePoint Online
• Legacy client documents on on-premises Windows file servers
• BYOD iOS and Android devices managed via Microsoft Intune
• External clients and opposing counsel receive confidential legal briefs via email
• Microsoft 365 Copilot deployed for 200 senior attorneys

yn.title: Yes / No
yn.body:
Northwind Traders applies two retention labels: Client Matter — Regulatory Record (Regulatory Record type, 7-year period) and Internal Documents (Regular Record type, 3-year period). A sensitivity label Strictly Confidential uses Assign permissions now encryption scoped to senior attorneys only.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true or No if it is false.

questions.stem: Northwind must detect documents with the same structural layout as their blank NDA template — without relying on keywords or regex patterns. Which SIT approach should they use?
options: A custom regex SIT matching NDA section headers and terminology
An Exact Data Match (EDM) classifier using NDA field values
Document fingerprinting based on the blank NDA template file
A trainable classifier trained on signed NDA examples
questions.explanation: C is correct. Document fingerprinting hashes the structural layout of a template — field positions, section ordering, paragraph skeleton — and detects new documents that share the same structure regardless of the data filled in. This is purpose-built for blank forms like NDAs, W-2s, and standardized contracts. A is wrong because regex matches text patterns and the question explicitly rules out keyword/regex approaches. B (EDM) is wrong because EDM compares document content against actual database values, which is useful for matter numbers or SSNs but not for structural similarity. D (trainable classifier) is wrong because classifiers identify content TOPICS from training examples; a classifier trained on signed NDAs would match documents 'about' NDAs broadly but could not reliably isolate Northwind's specific template structure.

questions.stem: Northwind must detect actual client matter numbers from their SQL database to eliminate false positives from similar-looking codes in documents. Which SIT type should they create?
options: A custom regex SIT with the MATTER-[0-9]{6} pattern and keyword corroboration
An Exact Data Match (EDM) classifier referencing the actual SQL database records
A document fingerprint based on a matter intake form template
A named entity SIT for financial matter identifiers
questions.explanation: B is correct. EDM hashes the actual matter-number values from Northwind's SQL database and uses those hashes as the match source — so a string only counts as a match if it exists in the source data. This eliminates false positives from unrelated codes that merely look like MATTER-XXXXXX. A is wrong because a regex SIT matches anything fitting the format whether or not the matter number is real — exactly the false-positive problem they need to solve. C is wrong because fingerprinting detects template structure, not specific data values. D is wrong because there is no built-in 'financial matter identifiers' named entity SIT — named entity SITs cover broad categories (person names, addresses, medical terms), not custom internal identifiers.

questions.stem: BYOD users access SharePoint sites containing sensitive legal documents from personal browser sessions. Northwind wants to prevent file downloads and printing from unmanaged (non-Intune) sessions without fully blocking access. What should they configure?
options: A DLP policy blocking SharePoint downloads on non-Intune-enrolled devices
A sensitivity label with Assign permissions now encryption on all documents in the site
A container sensitivity label on the SharePoint site configured to allow web-only access for unmanaged devices
A conditional access policy requiring Intune compliance before any SharePoint access is permitted
questions.explanation: C is correct. Container sensitivity labels on SharePoint sites include an 'Unmanaged devices' setting with three options: block access, allow limited web-only access (view in browser, no download/print/sync), or allow full access. Web-only meets both requirements — users can still read documents but cannot extract them from BYOD devices. The setting leverages Entra ID Conditional Access App Control under the hood but is configured directly on the container label. A is wrong because SharePoint DLP has no device-state condition — DLP inspects content, not device posture; recognizing whether a device is Intune-managed is the job of Conditional Access. B is wrong because file-level encryption applies uniformly to all access regardless of device — it doesn't selectively block download on BYOD while allowing it on corporate endpoints, and it doesn't gate printing differently per device. D is wrong because requiring Intune compliance for ANY SharePoint access fully blocks BYOD usage, contradicting the requirement to allow read access.

questions.stem: Northwind must send legal briefs to external clients via email. The emails must expire after 30 days and must be revocable after sending if the client relationship ends. Which technology provides BOTH capabilities?
options: A sensitivity label with Do Not Forward IRM permissions applied before sending
Standard Office 365 Message Encryption using the Encrypt-Only protection template
S/MIME certificate-based encryption with client-side key management
Microsoft Purview Advanced Message Encryption with expiration date and revocation configured
questions.explanation: D is correct. Advanced Message Encryption (an M365 E5 capability) is the only Microsoft email encryption option that supports BOTH time-based expiration (the message becomes unreadable after a configured date) AND post-send revocation (the sender or admin can revoke access to a message that has already been delivered). A is wrong because Do Not Forward IRM prevents forwarding/printing/copying but cannot expire or revoke. B is wrong because standard OME Encrypt-Only encrypts at send time but has no expiration timer and no revocation. C is wrong because S/MIME relies on certificate-based encryption between endpoints; once the recipient decrypts the message, the sender has no mechanism to expire or revoke it.

questions.stem: Which named entity SIT should you use to detect full person names across diverse European, Asian, and Middle Eastern naming conventions for GDPR subject rights compliance?
options: All Physical Addresses
EU Passport Number
All Full Names
All Personal Data Identifiers
questions.explanation: C (All Full Names) is correct. It is a named entity SIT that uses an ML model trained on multilingual name data to recognize person names across European, Asian, Middle Eastern, and other naming conventions without relying on fixed patterns. A (All Physical Addresses) is wrong because it detects addresses, not names. B (EU Passport Number) is wrong — it is a structured regex SIT for travel document identifiers, not person names. D is wrong because 'All Personal Data Identifiers' is not a named entity SIT in Microsoft Purview — Purview's bundled GDPR SITs have specific names like 'EU Driver's License Number,' 'EU National Identification Number,' or the 'EU GDPR Enhanced' bundle, but none is named 'All Personal Data Identifiers.'

questions.stem: In an Exact Data Match (EDM) sensitive information type, what is the role of the primary element?
options: It specifies the hashing algorithm applied to the database records before upload
It is the main sensitive field the SIT actively searches for in document or email content
It defines which users have permission to view EDM-matched content in DLP reports
It sets the confidence threshold above which EDM results are reported
questions.explanation: B is correct. The primary element is the central sensitive field EDM actively searches for in content — for example, the SSN column in an HR data table. Supporting elements (last name, date of birth) corroborate the match in proximity and raise confidence from medium to high, but the primary element MUST match for any result to fire. A is wrong because the hashing algorithm is fixed by EDM itself and not defined by the primary element. C is wrong because access to EDM-matched content in DLP reports is governed by RBAC roles, not by SIT configuration. D is wrong because confidence thresholds are set on the DLP rule, not embedded in the primary element definition.

questions.stem: A container sensitivity label is applied to a Microsoft Teams team. Which settings does it control?
options: Whether files in team channels are automatically encrypted when uploaded
Whether Teams meeting recordings are labeled when saved to SharePoint
The team privacy (Public/Private), external user access, and unmanaged device access for the team and its connected SharePoint site
Whether DLP policies apply to chat messages in that specific team
questions.explanation: C is correct. Container labels on Teams teams (which also govern the connected M365 Group and SharePoint site) control: privacy (public vs private), external/guest access, and unmanaged-device access. They govern the container itself — not files inside. A is wrong because container labels do NOT automatically encrypt files in channels; file-level encryption is a document-level sensitivity-label setting. B is wrong because Teams meeting recordings are labeled by meeting-scoped or file-scoped sensitivity labels, not by the container label on the team. D is wrong because container labels do not configure DLP scope — DLP policies have their own location targeting and conditions, independent of the team's container label.

questions.stem: What control does Microsoft 365 Customer Key provide that standard Microsoft-managed encryption does NOT?
options: End-to-end encryption of emails without requiring Outlook or Microsoft 365
Per-user granular encryption keys scoped to individual mailboxes
The ability for your organization to control and revoke the root encryption keys used for Microsoft 365 data at rest
Encryption of data flowing between Microsoft datacenter regions
questions.explanation: C is correct. Customer Key (BYOK at the Microsoft 365 service layer) lets the organization supply and control the root keys that wrap Microsoft's data-at-rest encryption keys for Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams. By revoking those keys, the organization can render its M365 data unreadable — even to Microsoft. A is wrong because Customer Key does not change message-level end-to-end encryption — it operates at the service storage layer. B is wrong because Customer Key keys are tenant- or DEP-scoped, not per-user mailbox keys. D is wrong because encryption of data in transit between Microsoft datacenter regions is a separate Microsoft platform capability and is not what Customer Key controls.

questions.stem: Your organization requires that classified documents cannot be decrypted by Microsoft, Azure, or any cloud provider — even under legal compulsion. Which encryption technology satisfies this requirement?
options: Azure Rights Management with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)
Microsoft Purview Customer Key (M365-layer key control)
Double Key Encryption (DKE)
S/MIME with an organization-owned certificate authority
questions.explanation: C (DKE) is correct. Double Key Encryption protects content with two keys simultaneously: one held in Azure RMS and one held by the organization on infrastructure outside Microsoft. Both keys are required for decryption — Microsoft alone cannot decrypt DKE content, even under legal compulsion. A is wrong because Azure RMS with BYOK still allows Microsoft operational access to the key when wrapping/unwrapping content. B is wrong for the same reason — Customer Key allows Microsoft operational access to keys stored in Azure Key Vault. D is wrong because S/MIME is a message-level technology between endpoints; it is not designed for cloud-stored documents and does not provide DKE's two-key model.

questions.stem: Unlike Microsoft Purview Message Encryption (OME), what is a distinctive infrastructure requirement for S/MIME to function?
options: Both sender and recipient must have Microsoft 365 E5 licensing
The recipient must access the message via Outlook on the web to decrypt it
Both sender and recipient must have valid X.509 digital certificates installed from a trusted certificate authority
S/MIME requires Microsoft Entra ID accounts for both communicating parties
questions.explanation: C is correct. S/MIME is built on PKI: both sender and recipient must hold X.509 certificates issued by a trusted CA and installed on their devices/clients. Without those certificates, S/MIME cannot sign or encrypt. A is wrong — S/MIME is not tied to E5 licensing; it ships in Outlook/Exchange. B is wrong because that describes the OME web-portal experience for external recipients, not S/MIME. D is wrong — S/MIME does not require Entra ID accounts on either side; it works between any two parties with valid certificates, including cross-organization.

questions.stem: A label policy has a default label of Internal. A user creates a new Word document and saves it without changing the label. Does this satisfy mandatory labeling?
options: No — mandatory labeling still requires the user to actively confirm the label even when a default is configured
Yes — the default label is automatically applied and fully satisfies the mandatory labeling requirement
No — the default label is applied but the user must confirm it within 24 hours before sharing
Yes, but only if the default label configuration includes encryption
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a sensitivity-label policy is configured with a default label, that label is applied automatically to new content at creation time. Because the document is labeled, mandatory labeling is satisfied without re-prompting the user. A is wrong because no extra user confirmation is required when a default is in effect. C is wrong because there is no 24-hour confirmation grace period. D is wrong because the encryption configuration of the default label is irrelevant to mandatory labeling — what matters is that a label is applied.

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of seed content items required to initiate training of a custom trainable classifier?
options: 10 items
25 items
50 items
200 items
questions.explanation: C (50 items) is correct. Custom trainable classifiers in Microsoft Purview require a minimum of 50 (and up to 500) seed items placed in a dedicated SharePoint folder before training can begin. A (10) and B (25) are wrong because both are below the documented minimum and the classifier will not begin training. D (200) is wrong because, although 200 is within the allowed seed range, the question asks for the MINIMUM — and 200 is far above it.

questions.stem: A label hierarchy has parent label Confidential with sublabel Confidential - Legal. A user selects Confidential - Legal from the sensitivity bar in Word. What is applied to the document?
options: Both Confidential and Confidential - Legal labels are applied simultaneously to the document
Only Confidential - Legal is applied — the parent is implied by the hierarchy but not separately applied
Only the parent label Confidential is applied — sublabel settings inherit into the parent
The user must first apply Confidential and then separately apply the sublabel in a second step
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a user selects a sublabel from the sensitivity bar, only that single sublabel is applied — Office records exactly one sensitivity label per file. The parent provides organization in the menu and may share visual marking/encryption settings, but it is not separately stored on the document. A is wrong because a document carries exactly one label at a time, not both parent and sublabel simultaneously. C is wrong because applying the sublabel does not back-apply the parent — the sublabel itself is what is recorded. D is wrong because no two-step apply workflow exists; selecting the sublabel applies it directly.

questions.stem: A Highly Confidential sensitivity label with encryption is applied to a Power BI semantic model. A user exports the dataset to Excel. What happens to the sensitivity label?
options: The label is removed — Excel manages its own label policy independently
The label is applied to the Excel file but encryption is removed for application compatibility
The label and encryption are both transferred to the exported Excel file
The user must manually re-apply the label in Excel after completing the export
questions.explanation: C is correct. When Power BI semantic models are exported to Office formats (Excel, PowerPoint, PDF), the sensitivity label AND its protection settings — encryption, content marking text, watermarks — flow through to the exported file. This is how Power BI's label-aware export keeps protection attached to data leaving the model. A is wrong because Excel does not maintain a separate label policy; sensitivity labels are tenant-wide. B is wrong because Power BI preserves encryption on export; encryption is not dropped 'for compatibility.' D is wrong because no manual re-application is needed — Power BI handles this automatically.

questions.stem: You want the MPIP Scanner to identify files containing sensitive information on on-premises file shares WITHOUT applying labels or modifying any files. Which scanner configuration achieves this?
options: Deploy the scanner with Policy enforcement set to On (Enforce mode)
Deploy the scanner with Policy enforcement set to Off (Discover mode) to generate a report only
Deploy the scanner with TestWithNotifications mode to preview labeling actions
Deploy the scanner in Audit mode with an instance count threshold set to zero
questions.explanation: B is correct. Setting Policy enforcement = Off on the content scan job puts the MPIP Scanner in Discover (audit-only) mode — it scans, identifies matches, and reports without applying labels or modifying files. This is the recommended validation step before enabling Enforce mode. A is wrong because Enforce mode (Policy enforcement = On) actively applies labels and protection. C is wrong because 'TestWithNotifications' is DLP-policy terminology, not an MPIP Scanner mode — the Scanner's modes are Discover (Off) and Enforce (On). D is wrong because 'Audit mode with instance count threshold zero' is not a Scanner configuration; the Scanner's behavior is governed by the Policy enforcement flag.

questions.stem: Mandatory labeling is enabled in the label policy. No default label is configured. A user composes an email in Outlook and clicks Send without selecting a label. What happens?
options: The email sends with an auto-generated None classification applied
The email is queued and held for admin review until a label is applied
Outlook blocks sending and prompts the user to select a sensitivity label
Outlook applies the most recently used label from the user's label history
questions.explanation: C is correct. With mandatory labeling enabled and no default label, Outlook blocks the Send action and prompts the user to select a sensitivity label before the message can leave the client. A is wrong because there is no 'auto-generated None' classification — mandatory labeling does not invent a placeholder. B is wrong because emails are not queued for admin review; the user is blocked client-side. D is wrong because Outlook does not silently apply a recently used label to satisfy mandatory labeling — the user must make the choice explicitly.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label is configured with Teams meetings scope only. Where is this label available for users to apply?
options: In Teams channels when creating a new post or announcement
In Teams group chats and one-on-one conversations
When scheduling or configuring a Teams meeting in the calendar or meeting options
In the Teams admin center when managing meeting configuration policies
questions.explanation: C is correct. Teams meeting-scoped labels surface in meeting scheduling and meeting options (in the Teams calendar and Outlook calendar). They configure lobby rules, who can present, end-to-end encryption requirements, recording permissions, and chat behavior. A is wrong because channel posts are governed by file/site labels and DLP, not meeting labels. B is wrong because chats are not meetings and do not expose meeting labels. D is wrong because the Teams admin center manages tenant Teams settings — sensitivity labels are administered in the Microsoft Purview portal, not the Teams admin center.

questions.stem: An event-based retention label has a 5-year period linked to event type Contract Expiry. The label is applied to a contract on January 1, 2025, but no Contract Expiry event is created. When does the 5-year clock start?
options: January 1, 2025 — when the label is applied to the document
When the contract natural expiry date passes based on the document content
The clock does not start until a Contract Expiry event is created in Microsoft Purview
January 1, 2026 — one year after label application as a default trigger
questions.explanation: C is correct. Event-based retention does not start when the label is applied — it starts only when an event of the matching event type is created in Microsoft Purview (via portal, Graph API, or PowerShell). Until that event is created, the retention clock has not started. A is wrong precisely because label application alone does not start the clock. B is wrong because Purview cannot infer a natural expiry date from document content. D is wrong because there is no automatic 1-year default trigger — the event is the only trigger.

questions.stem: You need to apply a 3-year retention policy to Viva Engage community messages. Which location should you select in the Microsoft Purview retention policy configuration?
options: Microsoft Teams — channel messages (Viva Engage integrates into Teams)
Exchange Online — public folders
Viva Engage — community messages
SharePoint Online — Viva Engage community sites
questions.explanation: C is correct. Viva Engage (formerly Yammer) has dedicated retention locations in Purview: 'Viva Engage community messages' and 'Viva Engage user messages.' These are separate from Teams, Exchange, and SharePoint and must be explicitly selected. A is wrong because Viva Engage is NOT covered by Teams channel retention — it is a separate workload. B is wrong because Viva Engage data is not stored in Exchange public folders. D is wrong because while Viva Engage uses some SharePoint storage under the hood, retention is configured against the Viva Engage location, not the underlying SharePoint sites.

questions.stem: A SharePoint site covered by an active 3-year Microsoft Purview retention policy is deleted by a Site Collection Administrator. What happens to the site content?
options: The site and all content are permanently deleted — site deletion overrides any active retention policies
Content moves to the Site Collection recycle bin for 93 days and is then permanently deleted
Content is preserved in the Preservation Hold Library for the full 3-year retention period despite the site deletion
Content is transferred to a SharePoint archive site created automatically by the retention system
questions.explanation: C is correct. Retention policies survive site deletion. When a site under an active retention policy is deleted, its content is captured in the Preservation Hold Library for the full retention period and remains searchable via eDiscovery — even after the site itself is gone. A is wrong because site deletion does NOT override retention. B is wrong because while the SharePoint recycle bin holds deleted items for 93 days, the retention policy preserves content for the full 3 years beyond the recycle bin. D is wrong because Microsoft does not auto-provision an 'archive site' — the mechanism is the Preservation Hold Library.

questions.stem: When is an Exchange Online mailbox converted to an inactive mailbox rather than being permanently deleted when the user account is removed?
options: When the mailbox has had no activity for more than 30 days prior to deletion
When a hold or retention policy is applied to the mailbox before the associated user account is deleted
When the organization has Microsoft 365 E5 licensing at the time of account deletion
When the mailbox size exceeds 50 GB at the time of account deletion
questions.explanation: B is correct. An inactive mailbox is created automatically when a user account is deleted IF a hold (litigation hold, eDiscovery hold) or a retention policy is in place on the mailbox at deletion time. The hold prevents permanent removal, and Exchange retains the mailbox indefinitely for compliance and eDiscovery. A is wrong because mailbox-activity history is not the determinant. C is wrong because E5 licensing does not automatically convert a mailbox to inactive — the hold/retention policy does. D is wrong because mailbox size has no bearing on inactive-mailbox creation.

questions.stem: Who can be designated as a disposition reviewer for a retention label in Microsoft Purview?
options: Only users in the Records Management or Compliance Administrator role groups
Any internal Microsoft 365-licensed user or mail-enabled distribution group
Only eDiscovery Managers with active content search permissions
Only Global Administrators and Compliance Administrators
questions.explanation: B is correct. Any internal Microsoft 365–licensed user or mail-enabled distribution group can be designated as a disposition reviewer in the retention label configuration. There is no special admin-role requirement to BE a reviewer (though managing the disposition workflow itself does require Records Management or equivalent rights). A is wrong because reviewers do not have to be in Records Management or Compliance Administrator. C is wrong because eDiscovery roles do not gate disposition review. D is wrong because Global/Compliance Admin roles are not required for reviewers.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of sequential disposition review stages that can be configured in a single retention label?
options: 2 stages
3 stages
5 stages
10 stages
questions.explanation: C (5 stages) is correct. A single retention label supports up to 5 sequential disposition review stages, each with its own reviewers and time window. After all configured stages complete, the disposition outcome (retain, dispose, relabel) is finalized. A (2) and B (3) are wrong because both are below the documented 5-stage maximum. D (10 stages) is wrong because Microsoft caps stages at 5 — not 10.

questions.stem: A DLP rule is set to Block, but allow business justification override. A user attempts to email a file with 15 credit card numbers externally. What is the user experience?
options: The send action is permanently blocked with no option to proceed
The file credit card numbers are automatically redacted before sending
The user sees a policy tip and can provide a business justification to override and send
The email is routed to an admin approval queue before delivery to the external recipient
questions.explanation: C is correct. Block-with-override shows the user a policy tip explaining the violation and offers a business-justification field. After supplying a justification (and optionally a category/reason), the user can proceed; the override action and justification text are logged in DLP activity reports for compliance review. A is wrong because overrides are explicitly permitted in this configuration. B is wrong because DLP does not auto-redact content — that is not an out-of-the-box DLP action. D is wrong because there is no admin-approval queue in block-with-override; the override is self-service with an audit trail.

questions.stem: Two separate DLP policies target the same Exchange email. Policy A (priority 0): block when credit card count exceeds 10. Policy B (priority 1): notify admin when count exceeds 5. The email contains 12 credit card numbers. What happens?
options: Only Policy A fires — higher priority policy suppresses all lower-priority policies for the same item
Only Policy B fires — it has a lower count threshold so it matches first
Both policies apply independently — the email is blocked (Policy A) AND an admin notification is sent (Policy B)
The email is blocked and no notification is sent — the most restrictive action wins across all policies
questions.explanation: C is correct. Across separate DLP policies, actions are cumulative — Policy A blocks AND Policy B notifies. First-match-wins applies only to multiple RULES inside one policy, not across policies. A is wrong because separate policies do not suppress each other based on priority. B is wrong because the lower threshold does not 'win' across policies — both are evaluated. D is wrong because notifications still fire even when a block is in place; the 'most restrictive wins' shortcut does not apply across separate policies.

questions.stem: A Windows 11 device onboarded to MDE is offline with no internet connectivity. Endpoint DLP policies are deployed. What happens to DLP enforcement while offline?
options: DLP enforcement is completely suspended until the device reconnects to the corporate network
Only block actions continue offline — audit and notify actions are paused
DLP policies continue enforcing based on the last synced policy settings cached locally on the device
The device is isolated by MDE and DLP is bypassed during the offline period by design
questions.explanation: C is correct. Endpoint DLP caches the most recently synced policy locally on the device (via MDE). When the device is offline, the cached policy continues to enforce — blocks, audits, and notifications all stay active. New policy changes do not take effect until the device reconnects and syncs. A is wrong because enforcement is NOT suspended offline. B is wrong because audit and notify actions also continue offline — not just blocks. D is wrong because going offline does not trigger MDE device isolation; offline is a normal state for an enrolled device.

questions.stem: Endpoint DLP must block printing of Confidential labeled files to all printers EXCEPT the corporate print server. What should you configure?
options: A DLP policy with a Block all print action and an IP-address-based exception for the corporate printer
A printer group in Endpoint DLP global settings containing the authorized print server, with a DLP rule blocking prints to all printers NOT in the corporate group
A SharePoint DLP policy preventing downloads of Confidential files before they reach the print spooler
A Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Attack Surface Reduction rule excluding the corporate print server
questions.explanation: B is correct. Endpoint DLP has 'Printer groups' in global settings — you define groups by printer friendly name, IP range, or USB device ID, then reference those groups in DLP rules (e.g., 'block printing Confidential files to any printer NOT in the Corporate Printers group'). A is wrong because Endpoint DLP rule actions do not take an inline IP-exception field; the proper construct is a printer group. C is wrong because SharePoint DLP cannot control endpoint print events. D is wrong because ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) targets exploit and process behaviors, not data-loss print controls.

questions.stem: You need Endpoint DLP to restrict uploads of sensitive files to personal cloud storage (Google Drive, personal OneDrive) while allowing uploads to corporate SharePoint. What should you configure?
options: A Web Content Filtering policy in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint blocking consumer storage sites
Sensitive service domain groups in Endpoint DLP global settings, then DLP rules referencing those groups to block uploads to restricted domains
A Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps session policy blocking uploads to non-corporate cloud storage URLs
A Microsoft Intune network isolation policy preventing access to non-corporate URLs from managed devices
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Sensitive service domain groups' in Endpoint DLP global settings let you categorize cloud-service URLs (corporate vs personal storage, approved vs unapproved). DLP rules then reference those groups to block, audit, or allow uploads to specific domain categories — providing granular control. A is wrong because Web Content Filtering in MDE blocks navigation entirely; it does not selectively manage uploads of sensitive content. C is wrong because the scenario specifies Endpoint DLP, not MDCA — and while MDCA session policies can also do this, sensitive service domain groups are the canonical Endpoint DLP mechanism. D is wrong because Intune network isolation is too coarse; it blocks all access, not just sensitive uploads.

questions.stem: A DLP policy must detect credit card numbers in Power BI semantic models and notify data stewards. Where should this DLP policy be configured?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps with Power BI connected via an API connector
Microsoft Purview compliance portal — DLP policy with Power BI workspaces as the location
Power BI admin portal — Data protection settings for individual datasets
Microsoft Purview auto-labeling policy targeting Power BI workspace content
questions.explanation: B is correct. Microsoft Purview DLP has native Power BI support — when creating a DLP policy you can select 'Power BI workspaces' as a location and configure SIT conditions and notification/restriction actions against semantic models. A is wrong because MDCA can monitor Power BI but is not the native Purview DLP path. C is wrong because the Power BI admin portal manages tenant-wide settings (label enablement, sensitivity-label settings), not DLP rules. D is wrong because auto-labeling policies apply SENSITIVITY labels, not DLP actions.

questions.stem: You want a retention label to auto-apply to SharePoint documents that contain specific classification keywords in their text content. Which auto-apply condition should you configure?
options: Auto-apply using a trainable classifier trained on example documents
Auto-apply using a KQL keyword query that searches document content for the classification terms
Auto-apply using a named entity SIT for the classification identifiers
Auto-apply triggered by a SharePoint column default value in the document library
questions.explanation: B is correct. Auto-apply retention label policies support a KQL query condition that searches document content and indexed metadata. When documents match, the retention label applies automatically — no user action required. A (trainable classifier) is wrong here because classifiers detect content categories from training examples, not specific keyword lists; KQL is the right tool for explicit terms. C is wrong because named entity SITs are designed for entity classes (person names, addresses), not arbitrary classification keywords. D is wrong because library-column defaults trigger labeling only at the document-library level, not based on a search of document text.

questions.stem: A Teams DLP policy is active. Users frequently share files via cloud attachment links (SharePoint/OneDrive links in Teams chat). What must you enable in the DLP policy to inspect the actual linked file content?
options: Add SharePoint Online and OneDrive as additional locations to the same DLP policy
Enable Scan cloud attachments in the DLP policy configuration to inspect file content referenced in Teams links
Create a separate SharePoint DLP policy with the same SITs targeting the same files
Enable session monitoring in MDCA for all Teams file link interactions
questions.explanation: B is correct. Enabling 'Scan cloud attachments' in a Teams DLP policy tells the policy to inspect the content of SharePoint/OneDrive files shared as cloud links inside Teams chat — not just the message text. Without this setting, the rule sees only the chat message and misses sensitive content inside linked files. A is wrong because adding SharePoint/OneDrive as additional locations applies DLP to those workloads separately; it does not connect the Teams chat detection to the linked content. C is wrong for the same reason — a separate SharePoint DLP policy is a parallel pipeline, not an integration. D is wrong because MDCA session monitoring is not required for this scenario; Purview Teams DLP handles cloud-attachment scanning natively.

questions.stem: Insider Risk Management sequence detection generates an alert when which scenario occurs?
options: A single upload event exceeds the volume threshold defined in the IRM policy
A user daily activity volume exceeds their personal 30-day behavioral baseline by a statistically significant margin
A user performs a specific series of activities in a defined order within a configurable time window
Multiple users in the same department exhibit similar risk indicators within the same time period
questions.explanation: C is correct. Sequence detection in IRM looks for ORDERED chains of activities — for example download → rename → upload to personal cloud → external forward — within a configurable time window. Individual steps may be benign; the sequence implies intent. A describes a single-event threshold, not a sequence. B describes anomaly detection against a behavioral baseline — a different IRM signal. D describes coordinated multi-user behavior, which is not what sequence detection covers.

questions.stem: The IRM cumulative exfiltration detection feature evaluates total data activity volumes over a rolling window. Which time window options are available?
options: 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days only
1, 7, 14, or 30 days
7, 30, or 90 days
3, 7, 14, or 30 days
questions.explanation: B (1, 7, 14, or 30 days) is correct — these are the four configurable rolling windows for IRM cumulative exfiltration detection. A is wrong because 1 day and 14 days are both supported, and the list is not limited to 24h/7d/30d. C is wrong because 90 days is not a supported option and 1 and 14 are missing. D (3, 7, 14, or 30) is wrong because 3 days is not a supported window — the shortest supported window is 1 day.

questions.stem: A user is designated as a Priority User in IRM global settings. What is the effect on IRM risk scoring for that user?
options: Priority users are automatically enrolled in all active IRM policies regardless of their department or role
Priority users receive a higher insider risk score weighting for the same activities compared to standard users
Priority users are excluded from IRM monitoring to reduce false positive alerts
Priority user activities are automatically escalated to the CISO dashboard without review
questions.explanation: B is correct. Designating a user as a Priority User in IRM boosts the risk-score weighting of their activities — their risk scores accumulate faster and they reach alert thresholds at lower activity volumes. This reflects the elevated business impact of activities by executives, privileged admins, or other high-stakes employees. A is wrong because designating a Priority User does not auto-enroll them in policies — they must still be in scope of a policy. C is wrong because Priority Users are MORE scrutinized, not excluded. D is wrong because there is no automatic CISO escalation pipeline — alerts follow the standard reviewer workflow.

questions.stem: What are IRM notice templates used for in the case management workflow?
options: Automatically notifying affected users managers when an IRM alert fires
Sending standardized communications to supervised users during case investigation — such as policy awareness notices or formal warnings
Notifying external regulators when a confirmed data breach requires regulatory disclosure
Generating automated weekly compliance summary reports sent to the CISO
questions.explanation: B is correct. Notice templates store pre-defined communications (awareness reminders, caution letters, formal warnings) that an IRM investigator can send to a supervised user from within the case workflow. They are dispatched manually, when an investigator decides to. A is wrong because notice templates do not auto-fire to a user's manager when an alert triggers — alerts and notices are separate constructs. C is wrong because IRM does not generate external regulator notifications; breach disclosure is a separate process. D is wrong because IRM does not produce automated weekly CISO digests.

questions.stem: Which IRM indicator detects when users browse to websites categorized as risky or in a restricted domain list defined by the organization?
options: Cumulative exfiltration threshold indicator
Security policy violation indicator
Risky browser usage indicator
Sensitive email forwarding indicator
questions.explanation: C is correct. The 'Risky browser usage' IRM indicator fires when monitored users navigate to domains categorized as risky (adult content, extremism, known exfiltration sites, etc.) — using categorization data from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint's web protection. It requires MDE integration to ingest browser signals. A is a separate indicator (cumulative exfiltration threshold). B is the 'Security policy violation' indicator — endpoint controls being bypassed or disabled. D is the 'Sensitive email forwarding' indicator — a different signal entirely.

questions.stem: A compliance admin needs to identify all files permanently deleted from a specific SharePoint site over the past 60 days using the unified audit log. Which audit operation should they filter on?
options: FileAccessed
FilePreviewed
FileModified
FileDeleted
questions.explanation: D (FileDeleted) is correct. The FileDeleted operation in the SharePoint audit log records permanent deletions (from recycle bin, second-stage recycle bin, or via Shift-Delete equivalents). FileRecycled records the prior step (move to recycle bin). A (FileAccessed) is wrong — that logs reads/previews. B (FilePreviewed) is wrong — preview operations, not deletions. C (FileModified) is wrong — edits to file content or metadata.

questions.stem: The MailItemsAccessed audit event records when Exchange Online mailbox items are accessed. What license is required per user for these events to be captured?
options: Microsoft 365 E3 with the Exchange Online Plan 2 add-on license
Any license with unified audit logging enabled at the tenant level
Microsoft 365 E5 or Microsoft 365 E5 Compliance assigned to the individual user
Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 for the mailbox owner
questions.explanation: C is correct. MailItemsAccessed is an Audit (Premium) event. Capturing it requires Microsoft 365 E5 or E5 Compliance assigned PER USER — the per-user license drives Premium audit event collection. A is wrong because Exchange Online Plan 2 alone does not unlock Audit (Premium) events; E5 or E5 Compliance is the requirement. B is wrong because tenant-level unified audit logging captures Standard events; Premium events specifically require the user-level license. D is wrong because Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 protects against email threats and does not license Audit (Premium).

questions.stem: When you use the keyword list format in a content search (one keyword per row), what additional reporting does this provide compared to a single compound query?
options: A geographic heatmap showing where matching content is stored across sites and mailboxes
Per-keyword match counts and location statistics for each individual search term
Confidence scores indicating how accurately each keyword matched the target content
Estimated eDiscovery processing costs broken down per individual keyword
questions.explanation: B is correct. The keyword-list format (one keyword per row) produces per-keyword statistics — match counts and locations for each individual term. This helps refine searches by spotting which keywords are over- or under-performing. A is wrong because Content Search does not produce a geographic heatmap. C is wrong because keyword matches do not produce ML-style confidence scores — that is a SIT/classifier concept. D is wrong because Content Search does not estimate per-keyword processing costs.

questions.stem: Which information is displayed in the DSPM for AI dashboard in Microsoft Purview?
options: Number of AI model parameters and training dataset sources used by Microsoft 365 Copilot
Sensitivity labels on content accessed by Copilot, oversharing risk assessment, and AI interaction activity metrics
Real-time token usage and per-user cost analytics for Microsoft 365 Copilot interactions
Specific prompt text entered by users in Copilot sessions and the full response content
questions.explanation: B is correct. DSPM for AI shows three primary signal types: (1) sensitivity labels present on content accessed by Copilot, (2) oversharing risk — broadly accessible or unlabeled content being surfaced — and (3) AI interaction activity metrics. A is wrong because the dashboard does not expose model parameters or training data sources — those are Copilot internals, not customer data. C is wrong because token usage and per-user cost analytics live in admin/billing reports, not DSPM for AI. D is wrong because raw prompt and response text is explicitly NOT exposed — only metadata and risk signals are.

questions.stem: Why is investigating a DLP alert in Microsoft Defender XDR advantageous over reviewing it only in the Microsoft Purview portal?
options: Defender XDR processes and surfaces DLP alerts faster due to real-time streaming pipelines
Defender XDR automatically remediates DLP violations using machine learning-based response
Defender XDR correlates DLP events with identity risk, device health, and email threat signals into a unified security incident
Defender XDR provides per-file encryption status details not visible in the Purview DLP alert dashboard
questions.explanation: C is correct. Defender XDR ingests DLP alerts and correlates them with signals from Defender for Endpoint (device risk), Entra ID Protection (sign-in/identity risk), and Defender for Office 365 (email threats) into a single unified incident with cross-product context. The Purview portal shows DLP alerts in isolation. A is wrong — the differentiator is correlation, not raw alert speed. B is wrong because Defender XDR does not auto-remediate DLP violations with machine learning. D is wrong because per-file encryption status is not surfaced in either portal — this option is fabricated.

questions.stem: Employees in the trading division are sending regulatory non-compliant investment advice in Microsoft Teams. Which Microsoft Purview solution should you configure to detect and review these communications?
options: A DLP policy targeting Teams messages for financial sensitive information types
A Microsoft Purview Communication Compliance policy using a financial regulatory communications template
An Insider Risk Management data leaks policy targeted at the trading division
An eDiscovery case with a Teams-location keyword search for regulatory terminology
questions.explanation: B is correct. Communication Compliance with the financial-regulatory communications template applies classifiers tuned to detect regulatory non-compliance language — insider-trading indicators, Reg FD violations, fiduciary conflicts, and inappropriate investment advice — in email and Teams messages. A is wrong because DLP detects sensitive DATA (credit cards, SSNs); it cannot infer whether advice is regulatory-compliant. C is wrong because IRM detects user RISK behaviors (downloads, exfiltration) — not message content compliance. D is wrong because eDiscovery searches existing content; it does not provide ongoing supervision or content classification.

questions.stem: The Legal and M&A Advisory teams must be prevented from communicating with each other in Microsoft Teams due to conflict of interest rules. Which Microsoft Purview feature enforces this?
options: Sensitivity labels with restricted user-based access on shared Teams channels
Microsoft Purview Information Barriers configured between the two organizational segments
Communication Compliance policies monitoring cross-team message content for conflict keywords
Microsoft Entra ID access packages restricting Teams membership for both groups
questions.explanation: B is correct. Information Barriers (IB) define organizational segments and prevent specified segments from communicating in Teams chat/channels, SharePoint sharing, and OneDrive sharing — explicitly designed for ethical walls between groups like Legal/M&A advisory and trading/research. A is wrong because sensitivity labels gate access to CONTENT, not communication between user populations. C is wrong because Communication Compliance MONITORS messages but does not prevent the communication itself. D is wrong because Entra ID access packages govern application/resource access, not interpersonal communication blocks.

questions.stem: A document in SharePoint has a manually applied Client Hold retention label. An auto-apply retention label policy targets the same site and runs. What happens to that document?
options: The auto-apply policy replaces the manual label with its configured label
Both labels are applied — SharePoint supports multiple retention labels per item
The auto-apply policy does not apply its label — the existing manually applied label is preserved
The auto-apply policy applies its label only if it has a higher priority number than the existing label
questions.explanation: C is correct. Once a retention label has been manually applied to a document, auto-apply retention label policies do NOT overwrite it. The manual label takes precedence — this protects deliberate human/compliance decisions from automated overrides. A is wrong because auto-apply does not replace manual labels. B is wrong because a SharePoint item carries exactly one retention label at a time; multiple retention labels per item are not supported. D is wrong because no priority-number comparison occurs — manual labels are simply preserved.

questions.stem: Once a document is labeled Client Matter — Regulatory Record, no user or compliance administrator can remove the label or modify the document.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Regulatory Record labels lock content permanently — no user, records manager, Compliance Administrator, or even Global Administrator can remove the label or modify the document. This permanent immutability is exactly what distinguishes Regulatory Records from Regular Records (which CAN be temporarily unlocked by an authorized admin). No would be wrong because it implies someone retains an unlock capability, which Regulatory Records explicitly do not allow.

questions.stem: A compliance administrator can unlock a document labeled Internal Documents (Regular Record type) to allow temporary editing.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Regular Record labels permit a records administrator to temporarily unlock the record, allow edits, and re-lock it. This admin-unlock capability is the defining contrast with Regulatory Records, which cannot be unlocked by any administrator. No would be wrong because it would conflate Regular Records with Regulatory Records.

questions.stem: If Preservation Lock is applied to the 7-year retention policy, a Global Administrator can extend the policy duration to 10 years.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Preservation Lock prohibits WEAKENING the policy: shortening the duration, removing locations from scope, or deleting the policy. It PERMITS changes that make retention MORE restrictive — extending duration or adding locations. Extending a 7-year policy to 10 years is a permitted operation. No would be wrong because extension is explicitly allowed under Preservation Lock.

questions.stem: Microsoft 365 Copilot will not surface a document encrypted with the Strictly Confidential label to attorneys not listed in the label permissions.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Microsoft 365 Copilot honors sensitivity label encryption — content protected with 'Assign permissions now' is only retrievable by users in the permission set, regardless of underlying SharePoint or OneDrive access permissions. Attorneys not listed in label permissions will not see the document in Copilot's grounding results. No would be wrong because it implies Copilot can bypass label encryption — it cannot.

questions.stem: When a user downgrades a document from Strictly Confidential to a lower-priority label, no justification is required as long as mandatory labeling is not enabled.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. Label downgrade justification is a SEPARATE policy setting from mandatory labeling — the two are configured independently in the sensitivity label policy. If 'Require justification for downgrade or removal' is enabled, the user must provide a justification regardless of whether mandatory labeling is on. Yes would be wrong because it incorrectly couples two independent policy switches.

questions.stem: An auto-apply retention label policy targeting the Northwind SharePoint site will overwrite a manually applied Client Matter — Regulatory Record label on existing documents.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. Auto-apply retention label policies do not overwrite manually applied retention labels by default — the existing manual label is preserved. On top of that, Regulatory Record labels are permanently immutable: no automated policy can remove or replace them. Yes would be wrong on both counts — both manual-label precedence and Regulatory immutability protect the label.
